questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Derivative with respect to a parameter
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a derivative with respect to a chosen parameter
questions.stem: A clinician models a tumour as an ellipsoid with volume V = (4 over 3) pi a squared b, where a and b are the semi-axes. Holding b fixed, what does the derivative of V with respect to a represent?

options.text: The rate at which tumour volume grows per unit increase in the semi-axis a, with b held fixed
The rate at which the semi-axis a grows per unit increase in volume, with b held fixed
options.misconception: reverses which variable is being differentiated

options.text: The rate at which volume changes when both semi-axes change together at the same speed
options.misconception: assumes both axes vary together

options.text: The second derivative of volume with respect to a, since the model contains a squared term
options.misconception: confuses the first and second derivatives

questions.explanation: Differentiating with respect to a while treating b as a constant gives the marginal rate of change of volume per unit of a. The squared factor on a makes this a first derivative that still depends on a, not a second derivative.
questions.hint: Name the variable that stays fixed.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Derivative with respect to a parameter
questions.learningObjective: Read a clinical slope as a parameter derivative
questions.stem: A bedside chart records infused volume against drug concentration: 10 mL at 1 mg/mL, 20 mL at 2 mg/mL, 30 mL at 3 mg/mL. What does the slope of this relationship tell the clinician?

options.text: Infusing twice the volume delivers twice the drug, so the relationship is strictly linear with no offset
options.misconception: reads the slope as doubling rather than a unit rate

options.text: Each extra millilitre of fluid adds exactly 1 mg of drug, so the concentration is the parameter derivative
The marginal effect of volume weakens at larger volumes, so the slope must be falling off
options.misconception: invents a decreasing slope with no evidence

options.text: The slope is undefined, because a relationship described by three points cannot be differentiated
options.misconception: denies differentiability from sparse data

questions.explanation: A straight line through the origin with slope one means the drug mass equals the infused volume times the concentration of one mg per mL. The slope is exactly that concentration, which is the parameter being varied.
questions.hint: Read the slope as the rate per unit parameter.

questions.stem: A colleague writes that the derivative of the dose model D = c V with respect to the concentration c is c. What is wrong with that calculation?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the dose is the product of the two variables involved
options.misconception: believes differentiating a product returns a factor

options.text: The derivative should be the total dose D itself, since D is what depends on c
options.misconception: identifies the dependent variable as the derivative

options.text: The volume V should be held constant, so the derivative of c V with respect to c is V rather than c
The derivative should be taken with respect to both variables at once, so no single answer is possible
options.misconception: believes partial differentiation is impossible

questions.explanation: Differentiating the product c V with respect to c treats V as a constant factor, leaving V itself as the derivative. A correct error analysis must also insist that the other variables stay fixed during the differentiation.

options.misconception: divides by the wrong variable

It is negative U over P squared, since P appears in the denominator of the model

options.misconception: uses a log rule for an algebraic quotient

options.misconception: confuses a level with a rate

options.text: Zero, because the creatinine level does not depend on the flow rate at all
options.misconception: denies the observed dependence

options.text: Roughly 0.8 mg/dL for each extra mL per minute of urine flow, in the interval studied
Exactly 0.4 mg/dL per minute, because the two levels differ by 0.4 mg/dL
options.misconception: confuses the level difference with the slope

questions.explanation: The slope over the interval is the change in creatinine, 0.4 mg/dL, divided by the change in flow, 0.5 mL per minute, giving 0.8. A slope over a finite interval is an average rate of change with respect to that interval's parameter.

options.text: A partial derivative with respect to a named parameter requires the other variables to be held constant

options.misconception: believes partial and total derivatives always coincide

options.text: It is the binding value B itself, since the model is linear in the free drug level
options.misconception: claims linearity in a nonlinear model

questions.explanation: The quotient rule yields L times P plus L minus P L over the square of P plus L, which simplifies to L squared over that square. The binding model is not linear in P, so the rate depends on the current value of P.
questions.hint: Apply the quotient rule and simplify.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Derivative with respect to a parameter
questions.learningObjective: Read a clinical trend with respect to a dose parameter
questions.stem: A haemostasis log reports clotting time of 12, 11 and 10 minutes against heparin dose of 0, 1 and 2 units. How should the trend be read for the dose parameter?

options.text: Clotting time rises 1 minute per unit, since the numbers increase down the list
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the trend

options.text: Clotting time falls 2 minutes per unit, because the total fall is 2 minutes
options.misconception: uses the total change as a unit rate

options.text: Clotting time falls 1 minute for each extra unit of heparin, giving a sensitivity of minus 1
Clotting time is unrelated to the dose, because clotting varies for many reasons
options.misconception: denies the observed association

questions.explanation: Clotting time fell by one minute for each extra unit of heparin, so the derivative with respect to the dose is minus 1 minute per unit. The negative sign captures the anticoagulant effect visible in the recorded data.
questions.hint: Divide the change in clotting time by the dose change.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Derivative with respect to a parameter
questions.learningObjective: Identify a missing denominator term in a parameter derivative
questions.stem: A report differentiates the model G = k A over (1 plus k B) with respect to k and gives A over 1 plus k B as the answer. What is the error?

options.text: There is no error, because the derivative of a ratio equals the ratio of the derivatives
options.misconception: believes ratios separate when differentiating

options.text: The denominator depends on k, so the derivative is A over the square of 1 plus k B
The error is that A should have been squared, since constants always carry a square in derivatives
options.misconception: invents a squaring rule

options.text: The error is that k should have been replaced by B, because only one parameter may appear
options.misconception: restricts the model to a single parameter

questions.explanation: Since the denominator contains k, the quotient rule produces an extra term and the derivative simplifies to A over the square of one plus k B. Separating the ratio into a quotient of derivatives is not valid here.
questions.hint: Does the denominator contain the parameter?

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Derivative with respect to a parameter
questions.learningObjective: Apply the quotient rule with respect to a preload volume
questions.stem: A model of cardiac preload is P = 4 L over (3 plus L), with preload volume L in millilitres. Find the derivative of P with respect to L when L equals 5.
questions.explanation: The quotient rule gives 4 times 3 plus L minus 4 L, all over the square of 3 plus L, which simplifies to 12 over that square. Substituting L equals 5 gives 12 over 64, that is 0.1875 pressure units per millilitre.
questions.hint: Use the quotient rule and simplify the numerator.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Derivative with respect to a parameter
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a parameter must be named when reporting a derivative
questions.stem: A clinician explains that the derivative with respect to a parameter measures the response of a model when that parameter changes and the rest are held steady. Why does this explanation matter?

options.text: It matters because derivatives can only be computed when other variables are frozen
options.misconception: suggests total derivatives are impossible

options.text: It matters because holding variables steady avoids the errors that clinicians usually make
options.misconception: treats the convention as a source of mistakes

options.text: It matters because a derivative computed this way is always more accurate than any other estimate
options.misconception: claims a partial derivative is always more accurate

options.text: It fixes which sensitivity is reported, since the model yields different values for different parameters

questions.explanation: Naming the parameter and freezing the rest determines the quantity being reported, and a single model produces different sensitivities for different parameters. Without that specification, two clinicians can compute different values from the same formula and both be correct.
questions.hint: Without a named parameter the question is ambiguous.
